subject: Biology
title: Ocean Zones: From Surface to Abyss
description: A 60-second lesson on Ocean Zones: From Surface to Abyss.

hook.text: The ocean is divided into zones by depth. Each one has different light, pressure, and life forms.

buildup.text: The sunlit zone (0–200 m) holds most marine life because photosynthesis works there.

discovery.text: The twilight zone (200–1,000 m) has dim light. The midnight zone below has none at all.

twist.text: The hadal zone—ocean trenches below 6,000 m—has crushing pressure, yet life thrives there.

climax.text: Pressure at the deepest point is over 1,000 times surface pressure—enough to crush most submarines.

punchline.text: Each layer is a different world, stacked on top of the last.

quiz.question: Why does most marine life live in the sunlit zone?

details.summary: The ocean is divided into vertical zones defined by light penetration, pressure, and temperature. The sunlit epipelagic zone supports photosynthesis. Below it, the mesopelagic twilight zone, dark bathypelagic, abyssopelagic, and hadal zones each host uniquely adapted life forms.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding ocean zonation reveals how physical conditions determine which organisms can survive where. The deep ocean remains Earth's least explored frontier, with new species discovered on virtually every expedition.
takeaways: Sunlight penetrates only the top 200 meters of the ocean for photosynthesis
The deep ocean below 1,000 meters is in permanent darkness and near-freezing
Over 80 percent of the ocean floor has not been mapped in high resolution

faq.question: How deep is the ocean on average?
faq.answer: The average ocean depth is about 3,688 meters. The deepest point, Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, reaches nearly 11,000 meters. At these depths, pressure exceeds 1,000 atmospheres, temperatures hover near freezing, and no sunlight has ever reached.

faq.question: What lives in the deepest parts of the ocean?
faq.answer: Amphipods, sea cucumbers, foraminifera, and bacteria thrive even in hadal zone trenches. Snailfish have been filmed at 8,336 meters. Life at these depths survives on marine snow, chemosynthesis, and scavenging. New species are found regularly in deep expeditions.
